slides.title: DPoP proof
slides.subtitle: Bind a one-use proof to an HTTP request, an access token and a protected key
slides.notes: Demonstrating Proof of Possession, DPoP for short, is how PAP makes sure a token on its own is never enough. In PAP the key is the Session Key: each Session has its own, and its thumbprint names the Session. This example makes a Session Key and a real proof, verifies it, and then shows a replay being refused.

slides.title: Why a proof
slides.statement: A stolen bearer value is **not sufficient** on its own: every request also needs a fresh proof from the key.
slides.notes: With a plain bearer token, whoever copies it can use it. With DPoP, each request carries a proof signed by a key the host protects, so a copied token without the key is useless.

slides.title: Who takes part
slides.diagram:
flowchart LR M["Model"] subgraph HOST["Your host, trusted"] direction TB H["PAP host"] -- "sign this request" --> K["Reactor key store
holds the Session Keys"] end subgraph CO["Company"] direction TB A["Company API
verifies the proof"] -- "record jti" --> X[("Replay cache")] end HOST -- "request, token, proof" --> CO HOST -. "policy booleans only" .-> M
slides.caption: The key never leaves the key store; the model gets yes-or-no evidence, nothing more.
slides.notes: The host asks for a proof covering one request. The Reactor key store signs it with the Session Key, without ever giving the key out. The company reads the key's thumbprint from the proof: that is the Session. The company verifies it, and remembers it so it can never be used twice. Off to the side, the model: all it ever receives from this exchange is yes-or-no evidence about the policy.

slides.title: What a proof covers

rows.label: htu
values: This target, without query or fragment

slides.notes: Each claim narrows where the proof works. Method and URL tie it to one request target. The token hash ties it to the token without putting the token in the proof. A nonce adds freshness from the company, and the jti makes it single-use.

slides.title: First use, then a replay
slides.diagram:
sequenceDiagram
  participant H as PAP host
  participant C as Company API
  participant X as Replay cache
  H->>C: Request, token, proof
  C->>X: Record jti until expiry
  X-->>C: Accepted
  C-->>H: API response
  H->>C: Same proof again
  C->>X: Record jti
  X-->>C: Already seen
  C-->>H: Safe replay error
slides.notes: The first time, the company verifies the proof and records its identifier atomically, and the request goes through. The same proof a second time is already in the cache, so the company answers with a safe replay error.

slides.title: What the example proves
items: A new proof and `jti` for every attempt, retry and redirect
A nonce challenge means a **fresh** proof, never an edited or replayed one

Replay protection is the server's job, **atomic** across its fleet",
        "One key per Session; an ended Session's key is **discarded**, never reused
slides.notes: Retries and redirects always get a new proof. When a company asks for a nonce, the host signs a new proof with it rather than changing the old one. And the company's replay check must be atomic across every server it runs, or a replay could slip through on another node. Each Session has its own key; once a Session ends, its key is discarded and the provider refuses to sign with it again.

slides.title: What the model sees

left.heading: Visible
items: Policy booleans: method, URL, token and nonce bound
Signature verified, the key names the Session, replay rejected

right.heading: Never
items: The JWK, thumbprint or private key

slides.notes: The tool returns only yes-or-no evidence about the policy. The proof, the token, the nonce, the key and everything that identifies it stay in host code.
